item.title: PHP Methods for Retrieving Remote File Size Without Downloading
item.description:
“PHP Methods for Retrieving Remote File Size Without Downloading”

How can a developer efficiently ascertain the size of a file hosted remotely using PHP, specifically avoiding the overhead of downloading the entire file body? Several established methods leverage HTTP headers, primarily the Content-Length field, obtainable via HEAD requests or specialized functions.

The core concept across most accepted solutions is executing an HTTP request that retrieves only the response headers, as these headers often contain the Content-Length indicating the file size in bytes.

item.title: URL Query String Array Formatting: Best Practices and Solutions
item.description:
“URL Query String Array Formatting: Best Practices and Solutions”

When submitting data via URLs, especially using GET or POST requests, handling arrays or multi-value fields requires careful consideration as no single, universally enforced standard exists. This can lead to inconsistencies across different server-side languages and frameworks. How can we effectively send and parse array data within URL query strings, and what are the common approaches and their implications?

Several methods have emerged to represent arrays in URLs. Let’s examine these techniques and their practical application.

item.title: Reliable HTTP Referrer Verification Strategies Beyond Untrustworthy Headers
item.description:
“Reliable HTTP Referrer Verification Strategies Beyond Untrustworthy Headers”

The HTTP_REFERER header, which indicates the URL of the page that linked to the current request, is notoriously unreliable for security validation. Client browsers supply this information, meaning it can be absent or easily falsified by the user agent. If security depends on confirming the source, what dependable mechanisms exist?

The Limitations of $_SERVER['HTTP_REFERER']

The primary issue is that this server variable is entirely managed by the client. As detailed in various security discussions, attempting to enforce site boundaries purely through this header is fundamentally flawed.

item.title: solved-how-to-fix-cors-header-access-control-allow-origin-missing-error
item.description:
“solved-how-to-fix-cors-header-access-control-allow-origin-missing-error”

Encountering the “Access-Control-Allow-Origin” missing error is a common hurdle for web developers working with client-side applications and remote APIs. This issue arises due to a fundamental web security measure known as the Same-Origin Policy (SOP). This guide provides comprehensive solutions to effectively address Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) problems across various server and client environments.

The Core of Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)

CORS is an HTTP-header based mechanism that allows a server to indicate any origins (domain, scheme, or port) other than its own from which a browser should permit loading resources. By default, browsers enforce the Same-Origin Policy, restricting web pages from making requests to a different domain than the one that served the web page. CORS provides a secure, standardized way to bypass this restriction when necessary.

item.title: Solved: How to Fix 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' Header Errors
item.description:
“Solved: How to Fix ‘Access-Control-Allow-Origin’ Header Errors”

What is the Same-Origin Policy (SOP)?

The Same-Origin Policy is a critical security mechanism implemented by web browsers. Its primary purpose is to prevent malicious scripts on one web page from accessing sensitive data on another web page. When your browser’s JavaScript code attempts to read data from a different server, the SOP comes into play, restricting direct access unless explicit permission is granted.
